notes: Perfect claim overlap (C81, C82, C83) on phase coordination analysis. Both agree that contralateral leg coordination is maintained and phase relationships are preserved, though with increased variability in slower flies.

High overlap (84.6%) on sensory deprivation findings. Both agree that proprioceptive feedback is not absolutely required for coordination, that tripod gait is maintained, but step precision is deficient. Reviewers noted findings as 'surprising' but accepted them.

High overlap (80%) on distinct neural programs claim. Both express uncertainty about whether three speed groups represent distinct neural programs. Reviewers questioned the rationale for three groups versus two or four, and LLM notes lack of direct neural evidence.

High overlap (76.9%) on gait continuum findings. Both agree that flies use a continuum of gait patterns rather than discrete transitions, with tripod gait occurring at all speeds but with diminishing frequency in slower flies.

High overlap (75%) on step parameter characterization. Both accept the comprehensive quantitative data on speed-dependent relationships for stance/swing duration, step length, and swing speed. Reviewers praised the extensive and detailed analysis.

High overlap (72.7%) on spatial footprint parameters. Both accept findings on stance linearity and footprint clustering differences across speeds. Reviewers explicitly noted these characteristics differ between slow and fast flies.

Moderate overlap (57.1%) on footprint alignment patterns. Both accept that footprint alignment shows distinct patterns at different speeds. Reviewers mentioned alignment as one of the characteristics that differ across speed groups.

Moderate overlap (54.5%) on fTIR method development. Both strongly support the technological innovation. Reviewers praised it as 'powerful and impressive' and 'a nice technical innovation,' matching LLM's assessment of well-documented validation.

Moderate overlap (50%) on speed distribution analysis. Both express uncertainty about the underrepresentation at ~20 mm/s and whether it justifies gait transitions. Reviewers questioned outlier determination and statistical basis for the break at 20 mm/s.

Moderate overlap (42.9%) on CPG-interneuron communication mechanisms. Both express uncertainty about mechanistic interpretations. LLM notes claims are explicitly speculative; reviewers' concerns about naïve CPG presentation suggest these interpretations need more careful framing.

Low overlap (25%) on speed-dependent sensory feedback effects. Both support the interpretation that fast-walking flies are less dependent on sensory feedback, as defects are more pronounced in slow flies. Reviewers explicitly affirmed this interpretation.

Claims C42 (foreleg leading role) addressed only by LLM as SUPPORTED. Peer R13 addresses different claims (C96, C98) about experimental approach comparisons, also SUPPORTED. No direct overlap for comparison.
LLM R5 addresses instantaneous speed analysis and wave-like patterns (C55-C58). No corresponding peer review result found addressing these specific claims about within-stride speed variation.

Peer R1 addresses foundational CPG and neural network claims (C1, C8, C9, C10) in the Introduction, expressing concern about naïve presentation. These conceptual framing claims were not separately evaluated by LLM.
